source: You mustn't think of it like some sad, one-sided, pining-away sort of thing, though. I loved him in a number of ways.
Above all, he was my dearest, truest friend.
I wanted to see his grief through to its sticking place. Now that he's gone, I'll leave Elsinore and return to Italy very soon, I expect.
And-- did you ever, with Hamlet...
Well, now. That's a story I'll take to the grave.
I never noticed all this about you before. I never looked closely enough, I suppose.
It is surprising what the eye misses when it does not understand what is possible.
Maybe that's why I never felt afraid as Katherine. Several of my men have seen me perform and never realized. I felt... safe.
They weren't looking for Bernardo, so they didn't see Bernardo.
I believe... if I could... if I could do anything... I'd be Katherine whenever I pleased, and Bernardo whenever I pleased.
At once both—or neither.
Can you not?
Not here. Not in Elsinore.
Then where?
I don't... know where else to go. I have my father's estate. It's mine now. But going there feels... wrong.
Come with me to Florence, then.
You'd like it there. Theater on every doorstep. And hundreds of Petruchios. Can't throw a stone without hitting ten beautiful men in their beautiful faces.
I want to. But... if I... think about it too heavily, I'll become too afraid to leave.
Then let's leave Sunday.
You heard me. Isn't it easier to make a snap decision like this? Pull a pack together and we'll leave. Two horses from the royal stables won't be missed for a few days.
That would be... so nice... to just vanish, and start anew...
I'll need to find time to say goodbye to Hamlet, of course.
And I to Marcellus. I owe him that much.
Let us part for now, then. On Sunday, we'll depart.
Wot's this about? Something wrong?
I have some news for you, old friend.
I'm... departing Elsinore. On Sunday.
Ah. War business? When'll you be back?
No. It's got nothing to do with that. This is a... personal endeavor.
I don't know when—or if—I'll return.
B-but—what about th'men here?
That's why I wanted to speak with you. They need someone capable and seasoned to lead them.
They need you, Marcellus. There's no man I trust more. And now the King will be relying on you, too.
I... knew in my heart th'day would come when you'd leave eventually. Jus' never thought it'd be like this. So sudden.
I'm sorry, my friend. I truly am.
I cannot speak of my reasons. But trust that I do this now to cause as little pain to everyone here as possible. Including myself.
T-then... it must be the right thing. Yer a sharp man, Captain. I jus' wish you well. I hope yer safe.
When I depart, I'd appreciate it if you didn't tell anyone where I went.
Aye. You have my word.
I'm sorry to trouble you.
Is it about my uncle?
Afraid not.
I'm leaving, Hamlet. Leaving Denmark, I mean.
Yes. Quite soon.
No. Sunday. But soon, I think.
What? Why?
What changed to cause you leave at a time like this?
I did. Or rather, I am not the man I was yesterday.
You know I am, and shall always be, your most ardent friend. But there's someone who needs me more right now.
And I need to follow that path where it leads, just as I followed your path here once.
I wish this weren't so sudden. But sometimes, haste is required in these matters.
Can you tell me earnestly that you aren't angry with me? That this decision isn't driven by our discussion earlier?
Perhaps it was in part.
But I think my heart was the last of me to catch up. My mind knew what your words would be before you said them.
I had imagined us having that conversation a hundred times. Truth be told, I thought I would feel surprised, or sorrowful, or frightened. But it was none of those things. I felt only peace.
And for that, I thank you, even as I say farewell.
Your blood and judgement are so well commingled. I've always admired that.
Go, then. Do what you must. But write me. From wherever you land, I mean. I'll come see you.
After all this business is over.
You know I will.
Good. Then let us not dwell further on morose matters.
Is it true, Bernardo?
These rumors I've heard--about you, about these... 'theater performances?'
Ophelia. How many people did you tell?
I thought... it would help...
You were wrong.
You told him, Ophelia?
I did.
What? From whom did you hear about that?
From Ophelia. She must have seen you.
What you heard is true, my lord.
I cannot claim it did not give me great pause.
But over the years, you've given me cause to rethink many a time.
When you devoted your life to God, I began to think for the first time about life after death.
The first time you defeated me in a duel, I rethought everything I knew about my footwork. And there was quite a lot to rethink.
When you spent your father's remaining years of illness at his bedside, I realized how little I truly knew my own father.
And when you, as a youth, defended me from being cuffed on the head by the bigger servant-boys...
I knew then I would forever owe you a great debt to your own defense.
And now that day has come.
You see, you reflect back at me a pure sort of introspection I never could muster.
My thoughts are crazed, jumbled, constantly shifting. You always seemed so self-assured by comparison.
But now I see you are uncomfortable. Am I wrong?
It feels like a private thing for you to know, Hamlet.
It is... difficult... to feel... so vulnerable.
I do not know what I ought to say, in times like this.
Nor I.
I never had a brother, Bernardo. But I always had you. Now, perhaps, I have a sister as well. Is that... right?
The specificities are, I think, irrelevant in this circumstance. I am, and shall always be, devoted to you, Hamlet.
And I in like kind.
Why were you afraid to tell us?
Your uncle...
He told me you would hate me. And Laertes as well.
He threatened to tell everyone in Elsinore. He promised it would ruin me.
That delusional fool.
It is a testament to how little he understands the people around him that he would say such a thing.
Don't worry about my uncle. If ever he threatens you, it will be summarily handled.
You have my solemn word.
Farewell, Bernardo.
My lord.
It feels as though a thousand bales of hay were lifted from my back.
I am grateful you brought Hamlet to me.
These rumors I've heard. Are they true?
About you?
About where you go at night, I mean.
From whom did you hear of such a thing?
From Ophelia.
Ophelia? But how...
At first, I could not believe I had to hear it from my sister—rather than from you, one of my oldest friends.
Laertes. If you're here to berate me... please.
Oh, make no mistake. I am angry.
I'm angry you didn't include me, a professional, in any of these so-called 'performances'.
Do you even have any real musicians in the pit? Or is it some country no-man on a fiddle?
What is the quality bar of this troupe? Surely not very high, if you haven't bothered to include me.
Don't lie to me. You've been acting for how many years? And I've played the lute my entire life!
You know that!
I could have been performing with you. Then, maybe, I wouldn't have to go to Paris to improve further.
The least I ask is to be included in any further such activities. Preferably preceded by—and followed by—wine and dance.
Honestly, Bernardo.
Y-you're... not... you didn't... come to mock me?
Why would I do that?
Claudius told me you would. That you and Hamlet both would.
I was so afraid.
Claudius said that?
Well, make no mistake. I haven't seen your performance yet.
If you deliver your lines without expression—if they fall flat and stale—rest assured. I will mock you.
I have no patience for dreadful acting. Life is far too short.
But as to the rest: I have known you since you were scarcely old enough to hold a sword. You have been a sibling to Ophelia, and to me.
Have faith in me, Bernardo. As I do in you.
Am I permitted to attend your next production?
But I must warn you... I look... different.
If you're any performer worth your salt, then I'm assuming petticoats are involved, yes.
Perhaps we'll have to line you and Irma up, toe to toe, and see which of you is more formidable.
In the interest of total honesty, my bet's on Irma.
Regardless, I'd better be off. See you on stage, Bernardo.
Er... L-likewise.
I am grateful you brought your brother to me.
...It is hard to trust you at the moment.
I thought you a friend. I thought you too stalwart to accomplish something like this.
Clearly, I was mistaken.
Regardless, this was not your rumor to spread.
I am not even certain how you learned of this in the first place, to be frank.
Do you understand? Tell no one.
...I apologize, Bernardo. I know it wasn't right.
But I wanted to—I thought—I could change your fate.
My 'fate' is not yours to change. It is between me and my God.
Never forget that. From now on.
I'm sorry. Truly. How can I make it up to you?
You may leave me alone with my thoughts for a while.
...Perhaps a long while.
...Lady Ophelia.
You've made me wait for a very long time, you know.
Quince? Where's... my... father?
Never mind that. I've put him on pause for the moment.
How have you been, my lady? And where have you been wandering?
Nowhere, other than my chambers.
Let's bare some leg, shall we? I saw you.
A familiar little lavender gown, trailing its way down to Castle Town...
And what did you find there? Hmm...?
I was meeting an acquaintance. It was nothing of note.
Nothing of note, she says! Ahh, but I don't believe it!
You've found something incredible, haven't you?
I mentioned once to you that I was here to find a lost item. Something of mine.
And now you've gone and done the deed, all on your own. So very admirable.
I spoke with Simona. I know who you are. Who you really are.
All of this—everything that's happened to me—it was just a game you were playing to get me to find that stupid book for you.
And, by the way, my thanks. This little adventure of ours has been truly delightful! Now—simply choose a fate and I can leave Elsinore forever.
You want me to use the book? Why? I thought you wanted it for yourself?
Because if you use the Book of Fates... it comes right back to me!
